scope: Relevant current prototype-phase messages from app-owned thread history; not provider transcript directories. Tool execution evidence is in files and run logs.

items.text: I’ll run the prototype phase in scratch storage, starting with contribution models and API round trips, then using those results to explore offline delivery and cache freshness. I’ll compare alternatives against the same scenarios and record what the experiments establish. Production code and live data will stay untouched.

The two first-stage experiments are running independently. The storage probe will keep “set my contribution” separate from “override the total,” so different product meanings don’t distort the comparison. The API probe will use real Rust schema generation and generated TypeScript decoders.

I’m preparing the failure scenarios alongside them: commit before response loss, restore from a backup, stale snapshots after clears, and cache refreshes that preserve queued writes.

The first failure traces show a useful distinction. Stable client operation IDs replayed unacknowledged writes after a consistent database restore; tying identity to the server generation paused those writes instead. Blindly assigning a new namespace could duplicate an effect.

The ordering probe also produced a counterexample to the clock proposal: an older restored snapshot received a higher timestamp and resurrected a cleared value. Revisions and restore reconciliation need to be treated separately.

The delivery and cache probes have run. They show why clock-based revisions can resurrect stale data, and how stable operation IDs can simplify restore handling.

The storage and real API-toolchain experiments are still running. Their completion will resume this thread so I can compare the results and finish the recommendations.
The storage comparison has finished. I’ll inspect its results and rerun it before selecting a model, with particular attention to legacy values whose provenance we can’t recover.

The storage rerun supports explicit contributor rows as the working model. It also makes the two “set” meanings concrete: setting a manual contribution gives 16 after the source changes from 10 to 12; preserving today’s aggregate-overwrite semantics gives 6.

There’s a migration constraint to carry forward. An existing signed adjustment can exceed 64 bits even when the final total fits. We need an exact internal representation for that adjustment and must keep its provenance labeled as unknown.

The restore probe exposed another useful boundary: safe replay depends on the operation. An unacknowledged additive observation can replay after a consistent restore, but a conditional edit must still check its original version.

That points to a smaller design: stable operation IDs for deduplication, plus separate version tokens for edit preconditions.

The storage rerun supports contributor rows. It preserves source corrections and keeps manual contributions distinct from legacy adjustments.

Storage, delivery, and cache observations are recorded. The Rust/OpenAPI/TypeScript experiment is still running; its completion will resume the final comparison and independent review.
The API experiment has finished. I’ll check its generated clients and runtime results, then combine the four experiments into a recommendation for independent review.

The API results show why this prototype was worth doing. Both generated paths decoded the exercised Rust outputs, but their input validation still differed. Tagged-enum fields, suppressed goals, dates, duplicate keys, and integer bounds exposed gaps.

Rust/OpenAPI with generated TypeScript types and Ajv is the stronger candidate in this comparison. It still needs explicit boundary rules. Decimal strings preserved large values, but their generated regex checks did not enforce the full 64-bit range.
